name: Emeka Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four and in the milking parlour by five. I manage the dairy and barley farm for the Hollins Cross co-op, forty member families own it, and I run a crew of five. Two hundred and twenty cows, a hundred and eighty hectares of barley, and a lot of standing in the rain thinking about feed bills. I've done it twenty-two years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing every cow by her walk. I can tell you number 114 has a sore foot from the yard gate before the vet's even parked. What wears me out is the paperwork and the meetings, the board wanting spreadsheets, and my knees on the concrete. My partner Grace says I talk to the herd more kindly than I talk to the board, and she's not wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At the union branch meeting there's always someone waving a magazine about robot farms, and I'd enjoy reminding them a cow doesn't care about hype. Online I don't post much, but I'd share it in the co-op group with a smiley face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to finish my working life the way I started it, which is a relief. I'm fifty-eight, I've got maybe seven years left in me on that concrete. If nothing big changes, I hand over to someone younger and go and grow tomatoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep the herd, keep the crew, keep putting the usual bit into savings each month, which is about four months of bills right now. Maybe I'd let our office lady, Dina, use whatever program helps her with the milk records, but I wouldn't touch it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the morning after a storm warning that never came to anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked about the board wanting spreadsheets. Would even a small amount of AI change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for me, no. Dina does the records and if a program saves her an hour, good for her. I've never used one of these AI things and I don't plan to start at fifty-eight because a salesman says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on your crew you'd still keep an eye on, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young Pavel, maybe. He's twenty-four and he loves anything with a screen, and if the hype dies he might get bored and leave farming. That'd be a shame, he's got good hands with calves.

S0.say: He'd tell the union branch and the co-op group that he was right all along, and enjoy reminding the robot enthusiasts that a cow doesn't care about hype.
S0.think: Privately it's a relief: he gets to finish his last seven or so working years the way he started and hand over to someone younger without upheaval.
S0.do: Keeps the herd, the crew and his monthly savings habit exactly as they are, with about four months of bills put by. Lets the office manager use AI for milk records if it helps, but won't touch it himself.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like a storm warning that came to nothing.
S0.quote: I'd enjoy reminding them a cow doesn't care about hype.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka is proud and settled, and the plateau simply confirms what he already believes. His resistance to new tools is personal rather than ideological: he's happy for others to use them. His only worry here is about a young worker losing interest, which says a lot about how he sees his role as crew lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union says: change is fine if the people doing the work get a share of it. I'd stand up at the co-op's annual meeting and ask who's going to own the machines and who's going to lose their hours. That's the public line, and I mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be the last one at Hollins Cross who knows how to do it the old way, and that's not a comfortable thing to be. The board would want robot milkers within a few years. I'd be the man in the way, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down with the farmworkers' union committee straight away, so the crew has someone at the table when the board talks machines. I'd also save harder, maybe an extra hundred a month, because I can see my hours getting trimmed before I'm ready to stop. I still wouldn't learn the software, I'd leave that to Pavel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared yet, but there's a knot in my stomach about the next board meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the board has talked about robots before. What's actually been said?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago a dealer came and gave a talk with slides of a rotary robot that milks without anyone in the parlour. The chair, a good woman named Ruth, said it costs more than the whole farm's profit for three years. They shelved it, but I saw people taking photos of the slides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the board did bring in robot milkers, where would that leave you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, as a man who cleans up after a machine and fills in its error reports. I've seen it on a neighbour's farm, the manager there spends his day looking at a phone that beeps when a cow refuses to go in. I didn't spend twenty-two years learning cows to babysit a beeping box.

S1.say: He would argue at the co-op's annual meeting that change is acceptable only if the workers share in it, and ask openly who will own the machines and who will lose hours.
S1.think: Privately he expects the board to push robot milkers within a few years, and he sees himself as the last person who does it the old way, standing in the way of change.
S1.do: Joins the farmworkers' union committee straight away to speak for the crew when machines are discussed. Saves about an extra hundred a month in case his hours are cut, and leaves learning the software to a younger worker.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a knot in his stomach about the next board meeting.
S1.quote: I didn't spend twenty-two years learning cows to babysit a beeping box.
S1.fieldNote: The gap between say and think is clear: publicly he speaks for fair sharing, privately he fears being made obsolete as a person. His refusal to learn the software is firm even though he knows it weakens his position. He frames the board as decent people being sold to by dealers, not as villains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in now, not after. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd sign every letter to our representative about a tax on robot labour. People would hear me on this, I'm not quiet when I'm angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be out of a job before I hit sixty. The co-op members are farmers, they're not cruel, but if a robot does my work cheaper and never gets bad knees, they'll take it. Four months of savings doesn't get you from fifty-nine to a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd cut back at home straight away: no new car, the holiday with Grace's sister gets cancelled, we'd stop helping our son with his rent. I'd go to the union and push for a deal with the board, written down, that nobody on the crew is let go without a year's notice. And I'd ask our daughter Amara whether we could lean on her for a while if it came to that, which would hurt my pride badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums, and I hate doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years before it arrives, what's the first thing that would go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Speed is what kills it. With two years, the board doesn't even have time to argue, the dealer just turns up with a contract and a finance deal. I'd have no time to save more than a few extra months, and no time to reach the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Grace that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, which is that I don't know what I'd do with my hands. She'd say we'll manage, she always does. Then I'd go out and check the calving pen at midnight because I wouldn't be able to sit still.

S2.say: He'd say loudly that the government must step in now, attend every union meeting and sign every letter to their representative calling for a tax on robot labour.
S2.think: He privately expects to lose his job before sixty, because the co-op members will choose a cheaper robot, and four months of savings won't carry him to a pension.
S2.do: Cuts household spending immediately, cancelling a holiday and stopping rent help for his son. Pushes through the union for a written promise of a year's notice for the crew, and asks his daughter whether the family could lean on her if needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, restless enough to check the calving pen at midnight.
S2.quote: I'd tell her the truth, which is that I don't know what I'd do with my hands.
S2.fieldNote: Here the threat becomes personal and immediate, and his politics and his fear line up. He blames the speed and the sellers rather than his co-op neighbours. Asking his daughter for help clearly costs him; pride is a big part of who he is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, but I'd say it with a plan. We'd have time to get the union and the co-op to agree a proper deal before the robots arrive. I'd be telling everyone at the branch: use these years, don't waste them complaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to sixty-three, and that's nearly within reach of my pension. So it's a race, really. Can I hang on long enough that the robots come for Pavel's job instead of mine, which is a terrible thing to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Grace and make a five-year savings plan, putting maybe a fifth of my pay aside instead of the little bit now. I'd push the union branch to get a written retraining fund out of the board for the younger crew. And I'd write to our representative every year, on the same date, so they know I'm not going away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. It's like a long hill, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year picture, what does having five years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes everything, actually. With two years I'm just reacting. With five I can save, I can organise, and I can maybe leave on my own terms instead of being shown the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years of warning make you change your mind about learning the machines yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds stubborn, but by the time I learned it, it'd be learning itself. Pavel can learn it, I'll fight to make sure he gets paid properly for it.

S3.say: He'd tell his union branch the same message as for the fast scenario but with a plan: use these five years to agree a proper deal with the co-op before robots arrive.
S3.think: Privately it's a race to reach sixty-three and near his pension, and he admits the uncomfortable hope that robots take younger workers' jobs before his.
S3.do: Makes a five-year savings plan with Grace, setting aside about a fifth of his pay. Pushes the union for a written retraining fund for younger crew and writes to his representative every year on the same date.
S3.feel: Anxious but workable, like facing a long hill rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: Can I hang on long enough that the robots come for Pavel's job instead of mine, which is a terrible thing to think.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn panic into strategy, and he says outright that time changes everything. His most honest moment is admitting he'd rather the robots took a younger man's job first. He still refuses to learn the machines himself, now framing it as pointless rather than just distasteful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to get it right, so let's not mess it up like we did with the supermarkets. Ten years is enough to write proper laws about who owns these robots. I'd say that at the union and I'd keep saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I'd be fine. I'd be retired before the robots really took over Hollins Cross. It's my crew and my kids I'd think about, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going much as I am, and keep saving steadily to retire at sixty-five as planned. I'd stay on the union committee and spend my last years pushing for a fair handover. I wouldn't buy anything new or change anything on the farm myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly for others. For me it feels almost like the AI Plateau one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years would take you to sixty-eight. Does this one even touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, if I'm lucky. I'd be gone by then, in my greenhouse, and probably calling Pavel every week to ask how the herd is. I wouldn't trust a robot with number 114, I'll tell you that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what would you be doing in, say, 2034, two years before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training my replacement and arguing with the board about the handover. I'd want it in writing that whoever comes after me keeps the crew's pay. That's the last thing I can do for them.

S4.say: He'd tell the union that a decade is enough to write proper laws about who owns the robots, and urge people not to repeat past mistakes with the supermarkets.
S4.think: Privately he expects to be retired before robots take over, so his concern shifts to his crew and his children rather than himself.
S4.do: Carries on as normal and keeps saving steadily to retire at sixty-five. Stays on the union committee and spends his last years pushing for a fair handover with the crew's pay protected in writing.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but mostly on behalf of others; for himself it feels almost like nothing changes.
S4.quote: I wouldn't trust a robot with number 114, I'll tell you that.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years his own risk mostly disappears and his concern turns outward to the crew. His sense of duty as a team lead is the thread through all five scenarios. He never once considers using the technology himself, even with a decade of notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is a law that says a co-op or a company can't let a long-serving worker go for a machine without a proper payout, a year's pay at least. And a pension you can draw a bit earlier without losing half of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Everyone talks about the jobs, but somebody should ask who notices when a heifer's off her food at three in the morning. I'm not against progress, I'm against nobody caring.

headlineQuote: I'm not against progress, I'm against nobody caring.
portrait: Emeka Nakamura is a 58-year-old dairy and barley manager who has run the Hollins Cross co-op farm and its crew of five for twenty-two years. He's a committed union man, proud, fond of his herd and openly unwilling to touch AI tools himself. He is calm when AI fizzles, uneasy with steady change, and alarmed by AGI in two years, when he fears losing his job before he can reach a pension. With five years he turns to saving and organising, and with ten he expects to retire in time and worries mainly for his crew.
biggestWorry: AGI arriving in two years worries him most, because he would likely lose his job before sixty with only a few months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A law guaranteeing long-serving workers at least a year's pay if replaced by a machine, and a pension he could draw a little earlier without heavy losses.
